issues.claim: The broker puts a copy of the message into every subscription, so every interested service gets the event independently of the others.
issues.problem: The Publisher-Subscriber excerpt only shows 'Each topic has a dedicated output channel, and each consumer can subscribe to all relevant topics' plus delivery-guarantee text. It does not show the wording about a copy per subscriber or per output channel, so I cannot confirm from the excerpt that this page supports the per-subscription copy claim. The generator notes ask for this check. 'Subscription' is Service Bus terminology, and the page may describe an input channel with a separate output channel per subscriber instead.
issues.suggestedFix: Cite a page that states the copy-per-subscription behaviour, for example the Service Bus topics and subscriptions page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-bus-messaging/service-bus-queues-topics-subscriptions), in addition to or instead of the pattern page. Alternatively, reword the explanation to the pattern page's terms (an output channel per subscriber, each subscriber gets its own copy).

issues.claim: Why do you run several instances of one service over one queue, and why do different services subscribe to one topic?
issues.problem: The hint almost spells out the contrast between scaling consumers and fan-out, which leans toward giving the answer away. The Russian hint has the same strength, so there is no drift.
issues.suggestedFix: Make it less direct, for example: 'Does the broker need to give the same message to every reader, or to just one of them, when the readers do the same job?'

issues.claim: brokers usually deliver at least once. If an instance crashes before it acknowledges a message, the broker delivers it again
issues.problem: This is supported mainly by the PeekLock and Abandon text on the Competing Consumers page and the at-least-once paragraph on the Publisher-Subscriber page. The citation is loose but the claim is correct.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally mention PeekLock explicitly, or leave as is.

issues.claim: call `BasicAck` only after successful processing, and limit the number of unacknowledged deliveries with `BasicQos`
issues.problem: In the current .NET client (RabbitMQ.Client 7.x) the synchronous IModel methods are gone. The channel type is IChannel and the methods are BasicAckAsync, BasicQosAsync and BasicConsumeAsync. A candidate would learn method names that do not exist in the current library. The generator notes flag this and the text does not resolve it.
issues.suggestedFix: Name the protocol methods (`basic.ack`, `basic.qos`) and the 7.x client methods: 'call `BasicAckAsync` (`basic.ack`) only after successful processing, and limit unacknowledged deliveries with `BasicQosAsync` (`basic.qos`, prefetch)'. Apply the same change in ru and keep the two locales in sync.

issues.claim: Кроме того, ограничение prefetch в этом режиме не действует
issues.problem: This is correct, and the confirms excerpt supports it ('there is no such limit by definition'). However, the same excerpt notes that some client libraries apply TCP back pressure, so 'the buffer can hold many messages' is slightly absolute.
issues.suggestedFix: Add 'как правило' / 'typically': 'the buffer can typically hold many messages, because some clients only apply TCP back pressure'.

issues.claim: Dead-letter exchange получает сообщения, которые отклонены без возврата в очередь, истекли по TTL или вытеснены лимитом длины.
issues.problem: This is correct per the RabbitMQ DLX docs: reject or nack with requeue=false, TTL expiry, and a length limit with drop-head or reject-publish-dlx overflow. The DLX page is not among the links, and 'вытеснены лимитом длины' is true only for certain overflow behaviours. It is not an error.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally add 'при переполнении очереди (drop-head)' and link https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx.
